title: People distinguish having a vote from having an effective say when governments appear unresponsive
source_unit: OECD Survey on Drivers of Trust in Public Institutions 2026 Results, Chapter 6: Political voice, barriers to participation and implications for trust in government
geography: 33 OECD countries and 5 OECD accession candidate countries participating in the 2025 Trust Survey, with OECD and accession-country averages reported separately

observations.period: 2025 OECD Trust Survey; perceived influence and political voice

denominator.unit: OECD and OECD accession candidate country contexts covered by the chapter; country averages are weighted and the OECD aggregate is an unweighted average of country averages

voting_influence.unit: percent average across OECD countries viewing voting in elections as moderately or significantly influential on government decisions

system_allows_say.unit: percent average across OECD countries confident that the political system allows people like them to have a say

own_participation_confidence.unit: approximately percent average across OECD countries confident in their own ability to participate in politics

mechanism.value: Voting can retain procedural legitimacy while failing to create a broader sense of effective voice

observations.method: OECD cross-national survey synthesis using weighted country estimates and unweighted averages of country averages; chapter analyzes perceived influence, participation, and trust.
observations.uncertainty: Country averages conceal within-country inequality and the aggregate is not a respondent-level pooled estimate; perceived influence is not observed policy responsiveness or actual political power.
observations.subgroup: Adults across participating OECD and OECD accession candidate countries; country and socioeconomic comparisons are reported where available.
observations.counterinterpretation: People may value voting as a meaningful accountability route even while demanding additional forms of voice; low perceived influence does not necessarily imply nonparticipation or democratic rejection.

observations.period: 2025 OECD Trust Survey; forms and frequency of participation

denominator.unit: OECD and OECD accession country comparison frame; country averages are weighted and OECD aggregate is an unweighted average of country averages

voted_last_national_election.unit: percent average reporting voting in the last national election

voted_any_election_last_year.unit: percent average reporting voting in any municipal, regional, or national election in the prior 12 months

petition.unit: percent average reporting signing a petition in the prior year

political_social_post.unit: percent average reporting posting political content on social media in the prior year

public_consultation.unit: percent average reporting participation in a public consultation in the prior year

mechanism.value: Low-barrier symbolic or expressive actions are more common than time-intensive direct engagement with officials or policymaking

observations.method: OECD Trust Survey self-reported participation measures summarized as cross-national averages.
observations.uncertainty: Voting may be overreported through recall or social desirability, and participation opportunities differ by country; frequency does not establish influence or representativeness.
observations.subgroup: Adults across OECD and accession-country contexts; activity rates are aggregate comparisons rather than a common individual participation sequence.
observations.counterinterpretation: Petitions, social posts, boycotts, and volunteering can have real political effects outside formal consultation, while low reported consultation participation may reflect limited opportunities rather than apathy.

observations.period: 2025 OECD Trust Survey; perceived effectiveness of participation channels

denominator.unit: OECD and OECD accession country comparison frame

public_consultation_influence.unit: percent average across OECD countries viewing public consultation as moderately or significantly influential on government decisions

townhall_influence.unit: percent average viewing townhall participation as moderately or significantly influential

government_adopt_consultation_opinions.unit: percent average finding it likely that government would adopt opinions expressed in a public consultation

officials_do_not_care.unit: percent average saying elected officials do not care about what people like them want

mechanism.value: The perceived responsiveness of officials matters more for trust than the mere existence of engagement opportunities

observations.method: OECD survey analysis of perceived impact of participation channels, expected policy adoption, and barriers to having a say.
observations.uncertainty: The results are associational perceptions; the survey does not observe consultation quality, government decisions, or whether opinions were actually incorporated.
observations.subgroup: Adults across OECD and accession-country contexts, with country-level variation in perceived responsiveness and participation channels.
observations.counterinterpretation: A consultation can have delayed, indirect, or agenda-setting effects that respondents cannot observe; low perceived impact may reflect communication failure rather than no institutional response.

observations.period: 2025 OECD Trust Survey; socioeconomic barriers to political voice

denominator.unit: OECD and OECD accession country comparison frame; subgroup comparisons by financial concern, income, and sex

no_time_barrier.unit: percent average identifying lack of time as a barrier to having a say

no_money_barrier.unit: percent average identifying insufficient money as a barrier

distance_barrier.unit: percent average identifying geographic distance from decision-making sites as a barrier

low_income_officials_do_not_care.unit: percent of low-income individuals reporting that elected officials do not care about people like them

higher_income_officials_do_not_care.unit: percent of higher-income individuals reporting the same barrier

women_officials_do_not_care.unit: percent of women reporting that officials do not take their needs into account

men_officials_do_not_care.unit: percent of men reporting the same barrier

mechanism.value: Material constraints and perceived indifference combine: unequal political voice is both a resource problem and a recognition problem

observations.method: OECD subgroup analysis linking financial concern, income, sex, and perceived barriers to political influence.
observations.uncertainty: Income and sex differences are descriptive associations; the data do not establish whether money, time, geography, discrimination, information, or official behavior produces the perception gap.
observations.subgroup: Individuals reporting financial concerns, lower versus higher income, and women versus men across participating countries.
observations.counterinterpretation: People with lower resources may have different expectations or exposure to government decisions; perceived official indifference may reflect actual policy conflict as well as communication.

related_sources.claim: Full OECD 2026 Trust Survey report and related chapters on institutional trust.
Prior OECD trust survey release for comparison with earlier waves.

boundary: This record adds a comparative route from participation and material barriers through perceived responsiveness, political voice, and institutional trust. It preserves country-average, survey, perception, cross-sectional, and non-causal boundaries: it does not measure actual policy influence, consultation quality, individual political trajectories, or a universal causal effect of participation on trust.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official OECD chapter was reviewed for the 2025 Trust Survey country frame, participation rates, perceived influence, responsiveness barriers, socioeconomic differences, and trust implications.
